newsitem.title: USA: Former CBOE chief says US options industry lagging.
newsitem.headline: Former CBOE chief says US options industry lagging.

text.p: Despite record volume growth, the U.S. options industry is lagging behind the growth of equity trading and must act soon to get more investors to use options or risk stagnating, Alger Chapman, former chairman of the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE), said Friday.

"The options business has not kept up with the explosion of NYSE (New York Stock Exchange) and Nasdaq volume over the past five years," he told industry members gathered here for the 15th annual options industry conference.
"We've got a tremendous opportunity to play catch-up," he said. "There are some things that must be done to capitalize on the dramatic increase in value and volume of the underlying equity market."

To battle this problem, the industry must bring down the cost of options to both investors and the firms that are distribution channels for options, increase marketing efforts, increase options training for new brokers and redouble its efforts to influence regulation in Washington, Chapman said.
Chapman retired from the CBOE in March after serving as chairman and chief executive officer since October 1986.
"Most firms see options as a relatively low profit margin product," he said. "Our business is plagued with small tickets and big discounts."
Options exchanges must find ways to limit costs -- "otherwise the firms will not support the business with training and marketing dollars that are critical to growth of the business," Chapman said.

He said in terms of increased marketing, the annual budget for the Options Industry Council (OIC), an industry marketing and educational agency supported by the four U.S. options exchanges and the Options Clearing Corp, should be doubled to $4 million.
The OIC, for its part, should include LEAPS (long term equity anticipation securities) in its marketing and educational programs, he said.
"LEAPS are the best way to bring new option customers on line," he said, explaining that their concept is easy to grasp and their two-year time horizon is perceived as much less speculative.
The options exchanges should also jointly create option education tools and make them available to brokerage firms at little or no cost, Chapman said.
"They ought to do it soon because plans are being made everyday to educate the brokers on something other than options," he added.
He said the exchanges have been successful "at the margin" in influencing industry regulation, but efforts need to be redoubled on several issues.
"The industry needs to participate in the legislative process much more than it has," he said. "We need an industry grassroots organization. We need a meaningful industry political action committee.

Chapman said if "every exchange member and everyone who earns their living from this business" wrote two letters a year "when the bell rings on an issue and contributed the equivalent of "one night out on the town with your spouse or significant other," the options industry would have both a strong grassroots organization and political action committee.

"We can't allow the 'let the other guy do it' attitude keep us from realizing the potential that exists to grow this business to new levels of customer service and understanding, to keep us from expanding the customer base and increasing the economic potential for firms and individuals alike," he said.
